transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-12
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 58m
Recorded by: Fireflies transcription
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Ben Torres (MajorCare SRE), Maria Lopez (MajorCare Platform Lead), Troy Nguyen (MajorCare Infra)

Summary: quick diagnosis on repeated CUDA OOMs and what looked like a "memory livelock" when batch sizes scaled, discussion of retry semantics causing duplicate work and exacerbating thrash, actioning a replay and log collection.

Shared artifacts referenced: CUDA retry playbook (internal): https://redwood.internal/runbooks/cuda-retry-playbook, benchmark sheet: https://redwood.internal/sheets/majorcare-gpu-bench.xlsx

[00:00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we pulled together a short playbook and wanted to walk through what we saw in your traces and figure out a deterministic repro path - Priya is gonna lead on the repro side.
[00:00:18] Priya: hi all, yeah, thanks. quick ask up front - is the failing host from this week the same machine referenced in the ticket? Ben?
[00:00:25] Ben: yeah that's correct, node-ml-07, same pool. We saw CUDA OOMs around 2am local on Wednesday and then the autoscaler kicked and things flapped.
[00:00:33] Maria: and just to reiterate, it's a mix of short chat-like requests and longer multi-turn notes ingestion, the latter seems to be when latencies spike.
[00:00:41] Troy: also note we've got a VPC NAT gateway that does outgoing calls for metrics, sometimes TCP connections time out and that overlays the picture.

[00:00:50] Priya: cool. so the logs you shared show three patterns: 1) hard OOM at allocation (cudaMalloc) 2) driver timeouts reported as "CUDA error: unspecified launch failure" which in dmesg is the tdr-like watchdog, and 3) a different case where GPU memory climbs gradually and never falls — that's the 'livelock' I'm calling out.
[00:01:12] Ben: yep. the second case looks like the kernel got stuck and the gpu driver reset. sometimes the process is killed by systemd cgroup OOM, sometimes the driver does a reset.

[00:01:25] Alex: what's the typical sequence? does batching step up, then KV cache grows, then we hit the OOM? or is it correlated to certain model versions / quant levels?
[00:01:34] Priya: good question. in our repros we saw: batch increases (auto-batching window) -> larger per-request key/value cache because long context -> combined memory for KV + activation + if model is 4-bit quant, some kernels allocate extra workspace -> sudden spike on a single token generation because of attention recompute paths. so it's multi-factor.
[00:02:00] Maria: the model in prod is a 16k context r-e-p-l-i-c-a we onboarded last month, but we've been experimenting with a q4_0 quant build that Priya helped us benchmark.

[00:02:12] Priya: right and q4 quant can surface different workspace patterns. note that some of the quantized kernels will use temporary buffers for packing — if those are malloc'd in GPU memory instead of host-pinned memory we blow up.
[00:02:30] Troy: are you saying the kernels could be doing device mallocs at runtime? I thought those were preallocated.

[00:02:36] Priya: most are preallocated but our fallback path sometimes does device allocations for attention caching when we switch algorithms mid-run, e.g. kernel fallback for long-seq attention. that's where we saw intermittent cudaMalloc failures.
[00:02:55] Ben: that matches an entry in the dmesg: "Out of memory on device allocation 0x7f..." repeated for the same PID.

[00:03:05] Alex: ok so one class of fix is to ensure preallocs cover the fallback working set and to tune batching thresholds to avoid triggering fallback en masse. another class is retry semantics — I've seen retries pile up and create thundering herd into the same host.
[00:03:20] Priya: yes. the default retry policy in some of your client SDKs is aggressive (5 retries immediate) which is bad when the error is transient OOM. we recommend exponential backoff with jitter and marking the error as retryable only after checking if it's a capacity transient not a deterministic model OOM.
[00:03:39] Troy: how do we tell transient vs deterministic? the logs sometimes just show "out of memory" without context.

[00:03:45] Priya: two heuristics: look at allocation size and stack trace — if the allocation request is tiny but OOM happens, likely fragmented memory; if allocation equals near-model-size, it's deterministic. also driver resets (nv-hostengine resets) followed by immediate success on retry suggest transient GPU driver flakiness.
[00:04:08] Ben: we also had a case where retries were routed back to the same host because our LB sticky session was still on and the request id wasn't preserved, so we just kept hammering that node.

[00:04:20] Alex: yep, that amplifies. recommended: client-side idempotency token + Redwood default routing with gentle rebalancing so retries can land on different hosts, plus server-side circuit breaker per-host.
[00:04:33] Maria: what's Redwood's circuit breaker default? does it open on N consecutive OOMs or on error rate?

[00:04:40] Priya: currently we have per-host circuit breaker that opens at 10 errors in 2 minutes or 5 CUDA OOMs, whichever comes first — but that's tunable. we can also add a temporary host quarantine window and route retries to a soft-pool (e.g., warm reserve).
[00:04:58] Troy: regarding KV cache, does Redwood evict keys when memory gets tight? we saw cache grow with long context and never shrink.

[00:05:05] Priya: we have a couple of eviction strategies: LRU-based TTL and per-request prefix hit caching. but if clients pin long-contexts and request full KV for each call, the aggregate can exceed reserve. you can configure per-tenant max_kv_bytes and fallback to context-window truncation.

[00:05:27] Ben: is there a cheap telemetry instrument we can add to detect the "memory livelock" early? something like a rolling GPU allocation delta.

[00:05:32] Priya: yes, we recommend a metric: gpu_mem_used - gpu_mem_prealloc, sampled per 5s with 1m rolling max; alert if 3 consecutive samples exceed 80% of prealloc. also track 'device_malloc_fail' counter and 'kernel_fallback_count' per host.

[00:05:52] Alex: I'll put those metric names in the playbook. also, for the VPC timeouts Troy mentioned: some timeouts show as client side connection timeout which made the client retry, but the worker was still doing compute and holding memory. that leads to leaked KV until the process dies.

[00:06:06] Maria: any recommended change to idle timeout or socket keepalive?

[00:06:10] Priya: increase server read timeout so that long-running generations don't get cut at the LB level; use streaming responses and application-level heartbeats. if NAT gateways are dropping connections, consider sticky keepalives or move metrics egress to a dedicated path.

[00:06:26] Ben: we saw one pattern with CUDA "unspecified launch failure" where dmesg had a driver GPU reset followed by a kernel panic. is there a way to isolate which kernel was running?

[00:06:34] Priya: if you enable runtime kernel tracing we can map the last dispatched kernel. we also instrument our runtime with a small ring buffer of recent kernel launches (name + grid dims + smem usage) which helps postmortem. we can enable that for a short window to capture the failing sequence.

[00:06:50] Troy: what's the overhead? we worried about instrumentation causing more pressure.

[00:06:54] Priya: minimal if the ring buffer is host pinned memory and we only capture lightweight descriptors, not full profiling. cost is <1% CPU and negligible GPU.

[00:07:03] Alex: ok, quick detour to batching: your autoscaler increases batching concurrency; if you get a sudden load burst the batching window can overshoot and create 2-3x effective batch that combined with KV leads to the spike. tune max_batch_size and prefer adaptive batching based on sequence length.
[00:07:20] Maria: do you have a suggested formula? like max_batch_size = floor(gpu_mem / avg_request_mem) - safety_margin?

[00:07:27] Priya: exactly. we recommend estimating avg_request_mem = avg_seq_len * token_activation_bytes + avg_kv_bytes; put safety margin 25%. we also recommend per-model batch caps and gated growth where the first request in a slot sets the expected work.

[00:07:44] Ben: what about preemption — can Dedicated instances be prioritized differently to avoid eviction?

[00:07:49] Alex: Dedicated capacity obviously reduces noisy neighbors; you can also reserve a warm pool to absorb spikes. for on-prem you can use cgroup pinning and set oom_score_adj so the serving process is less likely to get killed by host-level OOM.

[00:08:02] Priya: and for quantization footguns: some kernel implementations for q4_0 assume no packed workspace and will fallback to a slower but larger-memory kernel under certain sequence lengths; that fallback is the main culprit we saw.

[00:08:18] Troy: is the fallback deterministic by seq length or by runtime heuristic?

[00:08:22] Priya: both. it's mostly thresholded by seq_len and request batch size, but can flip if GPU SM occupancy is low/high because we have heuristics that pick a different attention kernel.

[00:08:33] Alex: so mitigations: 1) preallocate fallback workspace, 2) tune batching to avoid hitting thresholds, 3) tighten retry policy and add idempotency tokens, 4) per-host circuit breakers and quarantine, 5) better telemetry to detect mem livelock, 6) short-term: route retries to warm reserve.

[00:09:00] Maria: sounds good. can you write up the exact config keys we should change on our Redwood config?

[00:09:06] Alex: yes, I'll send a config snippet. Priya, can you mention the specific keys?

[00:09:10] Priya: sure — max_batch_size, batch_timeout_ms, max_kv_bytes_per_tenant, prealloc_fallback_workspace_bytes, per_host_circuit_threshold_errors, retry_policy: {max_retries, initial_backoff_ms, max_backoff_ms, jitter_pct} — note: I'll format these into the playbook as a YAML snippet.

[00:09:30] Ben: any immediate hotfix we can try? like lowering batch size on the pool?

[00:09:34] Priya: yes drop max_batch_size by 30% for 24h and enable prealloc_fallback_workspace. also change client retry to 1 immediate + exponential backoff thereafter.

[00:09:45] Alex: we'll send the exact CLI/Console steps.

[00:09:49] Maria: ok next, about retries creating duplicate downstream writes — we have a webhook sink that can process duplicates. do you support idempotency tokens?

[00:09:57] Alex: yes recommend passing idempotency_key; on server side we dedupe in the front proxy for a short window and return 409 if duplicate observed, or allow client to poll for status. we'll share docs.

[00:10:10] Troy: any notes about driver versions? we're on 525.x, is there a recommended driver or CUDA toolkit?

[00:10:16] Priya: we tend to recommend the long-lived driver 535.x for Ampere/RTX and CUDA 12.x stacks; some older drivers had known fragmentation bugs. we can check your exact dmesg signatures against a compat list.

[00:10:30] Ben: great. we'll collect logs and enable ring buffer for a day. one last thing — the autoscaler added nodes which led to CPU memory pressure as well. any cross-talk tips?

[00:10:40] Priya: ensure host-level memory cgroup for Redis/metrics isn't starving the OOM killer; and set oom_score_adj to protect the serving process. also prioritize GPU-bound scheduling to dedicated hosts.

[00:10:56] Alex: ok let's recap and assign next actions... (recap)

[00:11:05] Alex: recap: Priya will reproduce and produce flamegraphs; Ben will upload logs; Alex will share playbook and config snippets; we schedule follow-up repro session week of 4/20.
[00:11:20] Maria: thanks everyone.
[00:11:23] Ben: thanks.
[00:11:25] Priya: thanks, bye.
